stories.title: A high-speed train crash in Spain kills at least 68 people
summary: Early on 28 October, a Renfe high-speed train from Madrid to Seville hit the back of an Iryo train that had stopped near Urda, in Toledo province.
The Renfe train was carrying 397 passengers and the Iryo train 147.
At least 68 people died and about 80 were hurt, according to the regional government.
Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a train control system had failed on a 63 km stretch of the line, and he could not explain why trains were allowed to keep running.
why: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced three days of national mourning and promised to find out who was responsible.
It is the second deadly collision on the same line this year: in January, a crash between trains of the same two companies killed 46 people.

stories.title: Israel's election leaves no group with a majority
summary: Israelis voted on 27 October in the first election since the attacks of 7 October 2023 and the start of the war in Gaza.
With almost all votes counted, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc has 53 of the 120 seats in parliament, and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot has 48.
Arab-led parties won 19 seats, so neither side has the 61 seats it needs to form a coalition government.
why: The opposition cannot easily form a government without the Arab-led parties, but Eisenkot has promised not to work with them.
Netanyahu's Likud party claimed, without evidence, that the election was stolen, and the head of the election committee asked the security service to investigate reports of foreign interference.

stories.title: Lula wins a fourth term as Brazil's president
summary: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is 80, won Brazil's runoff election on 25 October against right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro.
Lula won by more than 4 million votes, although Bolsonaro had been ahead in the first round on 4 October.
Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, refused to accept the result and said he would ask for it to be cancelled because the Supreme Court let voting continue for two extra hours.
why: Lula first led Brazil from 2003 to 2010 and returned to power in 2023.
Analysts say the result is very unlikely to be overturned.

stories.title: Early voting surges before the US midterm elections
summary: Americans vote on 3 November in midterm elections that will decide who controls Congress.
More than 43 million people had already voted in person or sent mail ballots five days before election day, almost 10 million more than at the same point in 2022, according to an AP analysis.
A national average of polls gives Democrats 51.4 percent and Republicans 43.2 percent.
why: Experts say Democrats are very likely to win the House of Representatives, but the race for the Senate is much closer.
Control of Congress will decide which laws can pass during the last two years of President Donald Trump's term.

stories.title: Oil prices keep rising even though more oil is leaving the Gulf
summary: The price of Brent crude oil briefly went above $117 a barrel on 30 October, its highest level since April and more than 60 percent above pre-war levels.
Gulf countries are exporting more oil again, partly through pipelines that avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
But the cost of shipping oil from the region has risen to about $40 a barrel, around ten times the usual rate, because of insurance costs and attacks on ships.
why: October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial ships since the US war on Iran began, with 32 incidents.
Oil stocks around the world are low, and analysts say prices will not return to normal without a lasting peace deal.

stories.title: Hundreds leave a Russian-held Ukrainian town during a short truce
summary: Hundreds of residents were evacuated by bus from Oleshky, a town in southern Ukraine held by Russia, during a rare local truce.
The convoy travelled through Russia and Belarus, and the people crossed into Ukraine on 31 October.
The White House said US First Lady Melania Trump helped arrange the truce, and Ukrainian and Russian officials visited the town together to deliver aid.
why: People who left said there had been almost no basic food in the town since spring, after years of fighting.
Fighting continued in other areas, and Russian strikes left more than 200,000 homes in the Dnipro region without power.

stories.title: Hackers steal billions from the crypto exchange Binance
summary: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says attackers stole about $6.3 billion in an attack on 29 October.
The company believes a hacker entered its systems through the laptop of one of its engineers and then made withdrawals without permission.
About $3 billion has already been frozen, and Binance stopped all deposits and withdrawals for security checks.
why: Binance says users' money is safe because it will pay for the losses with its own money.
The price of bitcoin fell to a six-week low of about $77,600 after the attack.

stories.title: Nigeria tests two suspected Ebola cases as an outbreak spreads
summary: Health officials in Nigeria are testing two people in the northeast of the country who may have Ebola.
Both people have been isolated, and officials are looking for anyone they were in contact with.
Nigeria found its first Ebola case in more than ten years on 20 October.
why: The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo type of Ebola, began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in May and has caused more than 5,000 deaths there.
Cases have also been found in Uganda, Kenya and France, and there is still no approved vaccine or treatment for this type.

stories.title: Cyclone Arnab hits India's east coast
summary: Cyclone Arnab, a very severe cyclonic storm, reached the coast of Andhra Pradesh state early on 28 October and then moved inland.
More than 180,000 people were moved out of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha before it arrived, and at least three people died.
Strong winds and heavy rain destroyed at least 180 houses, knocked over many trees and left several areas without power.
why: Schools were closed and some trains and flights along the coast were cancelled.
Nearby Nepal stopped trekking permits for high mountain areas for three days because of the risk of heavy rain and snow.

stories.title: Report links almost 3 million deaths to climate change
summary: The Lancet Countdown, a yearly report on health and climate change, says about 3 million deaths between 2016 and 2023 can be linked to a warming planet.
Heat is linked to more than 500,000 deaths a year, and the report says 68 percent of those are caused by human-driven climate change.
Heat also cost 573 billion hours of work in 2025, mostly in poorer countries.
why: The researchers want climate change to be declared a global health emergency.
The report says cleaner energy is already saving lives, with about 400,000 fewer deaths from air pollution in 2023 than in 2016.
It was published before the COP31 climate talks in Türkiye in November.

stories.title: Astronomers find what may be a new dwarf planet beyond Neptune
summary: Scientists from Harvard and the Smithsonian have found a large, bright object in the Kuiper Belt, the icy region beyond Neptune.
It is probably between 600 and 1,500 kilometres across, so it would be one of the seven largest known objects in the outer solar system.
It was found in pictures from the Rubin Observatory in Chile, which scans the whole visible sky about every three nights.
why: The object stayed hidden because the Milky Way, one of the brightest parts of the night sky, is behind it.
It is bright enough for skilled amateur astronomers to see, and more observations are needed to measure its real size.

stories.title: The Netherlands will not take part in Eurovision 2027
summary: The Dutch public broadcaster NPO says it will not send a singer to the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027 because of disagreement over Israel taking part.
Its media director, Jurre Bosman, said Israel's participation divides people in the Netherlands.
The 2027 contest will be held in Burgas, Bulgaria, after the Bulgarian singer Dara won this year's contest with the song Bangaranga.
why: The Netherlands, Spain, Ireland, Slovenia and Iceland all boycotted the 2026 contest in Vienna, and Ireland will also miss the 2027 contest.
Dutch viewers will still be able to watch the show on public television.

stories.title: The Milwaukee Brewers win their first World Series
summary: The Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 on 28 October to win baseball's World Series by four games to one.
Pitcher Jacob Misiorowski did not allow a run in almost six innings, and William Contreras was named the most valuable player of the series.
It is the first World Series title for the club, which moved to Milwaukee in 1970.
why: The Brewers had the best record in the major leagues this season, with 103 wins.
It was the first World Series since 1991 between two teams that spend less than most other clubs on player salaries.

stories.title: Jumping spiders have a sleep stage like the one in which people dream
summary: Researchers filmed Australian fringed jumping spiders at night and found that they go through at least two stages of sleep.
In one stage, the spiders curl their legs, twitch and move their eyes, much like people in REM sleep, when most dreaming happens.
When a loud noise woke them in this stage, the spiders reacted slowly, and some did not react at all.
why: Spiders and animals with backbones split from each other about 500 million years ago, so the basic pattern of sleep may be much older than scientists thought.
The study, by researchers from the University of Bonn in Germany and others, was published on 27 October.

stories.title: Iran warns US warships to stay away as Trump considers new attacks
summary: Iran's top military commander, Ali Abdollahi, said Iran can hit any US ship near its waters.
At a rally in Florida, President Donald Trump said the US might start another big bombing campaign, or keep up its naval blockade and sanctions.
Ships near the Strait of Hormuz are still being attacked, and the price of Brent oil rose to about $117 a barrel, the highest since April.
why: The war began with a US and Israeli attack on Iran on 28 February, and talks to end it have made no clear progress.
Foreign ministers from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Egypt and four European countries met in Istanbul and warned that new attacks would widen the war.

stories.title: Serbia's Vucic admits defeat as a student-led list wins the election
summary: Aleksandar Vucic, who has led Serbia for more than a decade, admitted that his party lost Sunday's parliamentary election.
He said the Students' List would win 135 to 140 of the 250 seats, while his Serbian Progressive Party would get about 105.
Supporters of the winners filled the streets of Belgrade and other cities, and turnout was expected to be around 70%, the highest since 2000.
why: The protest movement began in 2024, after a concrete roof at a train station in Novi Sad fell and killed 16 people.
Protesters blamed the disaster on corruption, which Vucic and his party deny.

stories.title: Brazil chooses between Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro in a close runoff
summary: Brazilians voted on Sunday in a second round between President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro won 47% in the first round and Lula 45%, and the last polls showed a very close race.
On the final day of campaigning, both men held big rallies in Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo.
why: Lula, a left-wing leader, wants a fourth term, while Bolsonaro, a right-wing ally of Donald Trump, has promised to build more prisons and cut government spending.
His father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year prison sentence for trying to stay in power after losing the 2022 election.

stories.title: Hundreds of thousands march in France over living costs and schools
summary: French officials said 410,000 people protested across the country on Saturday, including 110,000 in Paris, while unions said the numbers were almost twice as high.
Police used tear gas and water cannon in Paris in the evening, and nearly 1,000 people were arrested nationwide.
More than 70,000 police officers were on duty, and the Louvre museum closed for the day.
why: The movement began in September, when high school students blocked schools over old buildings and a lack of teachers.
It has grown into a wider protest against rising prices, inequality and President Emmanuel Macron, six months before a presidential election.

stories.title: Israel closes Hebron, and about 2,000 people must leave their homes
summary: Israel closed the West Bank city of Hebron after two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at an army base on Friday.
Israel's defence minister said about 2,000 people had been told to leave their homes and could not return for now.
People in the city of about 200,000 cannot enter or leave, and Israeli forces arrested about 70 Palestinians in raids across the West Bank.
why: The Palestinian Authority and the Israeli rights group B'Tselem called the measures collective punishment, and the UN chief said he was deeply concerned.
Israel holds a general election on 27 October.

stories.title: Serious flaws in PHP, found with AI, push websites offline
summary: The makers of PHP, a programming language used by more than 70% of websites, released urgent fixes after details of two serious flaws leaked online.
The flaws could let hackers run their own code on a website and steal data such as passwords.
Government websites in the Netherlands, Finland, France and Belgium were taken offline as a precaution, and Wikipedia also shut down some systems.
why: Two security companies, Calif and Wiz, found the flaws with the help of AI, and say they had been hidden in PHP's code for more than ten years.
Website owners are being told to update PHP immediately.

stories.title: Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returns to Venezuela
summary: Maria Corina Machado, who won the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize, returned to Venezuela on Sunday after almost a year abroad.
She did not say where she was or how she returned, but wrote online that she was with the people.
Another opposition leader, Edmundo Gonzalez, said he would join her very soon.
why: Venezuela has been led by acting president Delcy Rodriguez since US forces captured Nicolas Maduro in January, and no presidential election has been planned.
Machado and her allies want a date for an election.

stories.title: China's economy grows faster than expected thanks to tech exports
summary: China's economy grew by 4.5% from July to September compared with a year earlier, faster than most experts had forecast.
Growth rose from 4.3% in the previous three months, helped by strong sales of computer chips and other tech goods abroad during the AI boom.
But people at home are spending little: retail sales grew by only 1.1% in September.
why: The government's growth target for 2026 is 4.5% to 5%, one of the lowest in decades outside the COVID years.
A weak property market is still slowing the world's second-biggest economy.

stories.title: A personal cancer vaccine cuts the risk of melanoma returning
summary: A vaccine made from each patient's own tumour lowered the risk of melanoma returning by 42% in a large trial led from Australia.
The trial included 1,137 people at very high risk at 157 sites around the world, and compared the vaccine plus an existing immune treatment with the immune treatment alone.
Lead researcher Georgina Long called the results transformational.
why: The vaccine, made by Moderna and MSD, does not prevent cancer, and it could take several years before it is approved.
Australia has the highest rate of melanoma in the world, and experts say protection from the sun is still the best way to prevent it.

stories.title: Measles spreads fast among the Amish in Pennsylvania
summary: Pennsylvania has had more than 1,300 measles cases since April, its worst outbreak in more than 30 years.
At least six people have died, including two babies, and none of them had been vaccinated.
Officials say low vaccination rates in Amish communities, where families are large and people often meet at church, have helped the virus spread.
why: The US has had more than 4,500 cases this year, the most since 1991.
Governor Josh Shapiro has clashed with US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has raised doubts about vaccines.

stories.title: UN report says the world can no longer avoid passing 1.5 degrees of warming
summary: A yearly UN report says current policies put the planet on track for 2.8 degrees Celsius of warming by 2100.
If countries keep their newest promises, warming would be about 2.6 degrees, still far above the goals of the Paris Agreement.
The report says US emissions grew far more than those of other big economies, partly because of power demand from data centres and support for coal.
why: The report says it is still possible to bring warming back below 1.5 degrees by 2100, but only with very fast cuts in emissions.
Clean energy has grown faster than expected: solar power has been built seven times faster than predicted ten years ago.

stories.title: Japan launches a mission to bring back soil from a moon of Mars
summary: Japan's space agency, JAXA, launched its MMX spacecraft on an H3 rocket from the Tanegashima Space Center.
It should reach Mars in August 2027 and try to become the first spacecraft to land on Phobos, the larger of Mars's two moons.
It plans to collect about 10 grams of material and send it back to Earth, landing in Australia in 2031.
why: A small rover built by the French and German space agencies will also be dropped onto Phobos, and NASA will receive at least 15% of the samples.

stories.title: Antonelli wins in Texas and is near the Formula 1 title
summary: Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli won the United States Grand Prix in Austin after starting in first place.
Charles Leclerc of Ferrari was second and Max Verstappen of Red Bull third, while Australia's Oscar Piastri finished seventh.
Antonelli now leads the championship by 123 points, with five races still to go.
why: He could not quite win the title in Texas, but he needs only a few more points to become world champion.

stories.title: The US government fights a plan to sell objects from the Titanic
summary: RMS Titanic Inc, the company with the rights to the Titanic wreck, wants to auction more than 100 objects, including jewellery, cutlery and a bronze statue from the ship's famous staircase.
A US judge paused the sale in August, and the company has appealed.
The US ocean agency NOAA says the items should stay together as one collection for the public.
why: The company says these items, found in 1987, are not covered by the court's rules.
The Titanic hit an iceberg and sank in April 1912, and about 1,500 people died.

stories.title: More ships are hit near the Strait of Hormuz as Iran talks stall
summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say a large oil tanker hit a sea mine and caught fire after using a route they had not allowed.
The UAE coastguard rescued 22 sailors from another burning tanker, and US forces disabled a cargo ship near Oman.
Since July, the US has turned back 135 ships as part of its blockade of Iran's ports.
why: About one fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through the strait.
Talks to end the war, which began in February, have made no progress, and few people expect a deal before the US elections on 3 November.

stories.title: Zelenskyy says Russia broke an energy ceasefire announced by Trump
summary: US President Donald Trump said Russia and Ukraine had both agreed to stop attacking each other's energy sites.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he first heard about it from the news.
He said Russia attacked anyway, including a power plant in Kharkiv on Sunday evening.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine would stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Russia stopped its attacks too.
why: Attacks on power plants and refineries have pushed up energy prices around the world.
The Kremlin did not comment on the ceasefire at first.

stories.title: War and debt top the agenda as the IMF and World Bank meet in Bangkok
summary: Finance officials from around the world are meeting in Bangkok this week for the yearly IMF and World Bank meetings.
About 18,000 people have registered, but US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is not going.
The IMF expects the world economy to grow by about 3% in 2026.
why: The war on Iran has caused a huge shock to energy supplies and is pushing prices up.
Government debt is at its highest level since World War II, and poorer countries must pay about $400 billion to foreign lenders this year.

stories.title: US government investigates five TV networks over a White House news boycott
summary: The US Justice Department is investigating ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.
The networks stopped covering the White House together after reporters from three news groups lost their passes in September.
A judge ruled the ban was probably against the constitution, and the passes were returned on 24 September.
Officials say a boycott by competing companies can break competition law.
why: It is the latest dispute between the Trump administration and major news organisations.

stories.title: Drone attack shuts down a data centre of Russian tech company Yandex
summary: Yandex says its data centre in Vladimir, east of Moscow, was completely shut down after a drone attack on Sunday.
No one was hurt, but several of its online services stopped working.
It was the third attack on a Yandex data centre in about a week.
why: Yandex is a leader in artificial intelligence in Russia, and Russia and Ukraine are both attacking each other's technology systems.

stories.title: The winning video in a microscope contest was made with AI
summary: Nikon has removed the winner of its Small World In Motion contest for microscope videos.
The video showed tiny hairs inside the airways of a child with a rare disease, but parts of it were made with AI.
Experts had said online that the cells did not look real.
Vietnamese researcher Nguyen Nam Nhat, whose video of a tiny worm came second, is now the winner.
why: Scientists worry that fake images could confuse the public about real diseases.

stories.title: Shrinking wetlands put Australia's southern brolgas at risk
summary: A study from Macquarie University found that brolgas in southern Australia are now genetically different from those in the north.
Genetic variety among the birds in Victoria has also fallen, and only about 1,000 are left there.
Researchers say the loss of wetlands, where the tall birds breed and feed, is the main cause.
why: Less genetic variety makes it harder for a group of animals to survive extreme events such as droughts.
Work to bring water back to some wetlands has already helped brolgas return.

stories.title: Russian attack kills 20 in a Ukrainian city as peace talks are held in Miami
summary: A Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia early on Saturday killed 20 people, including three children.
Officials said Russia hit several places at the same time, and part of an apartment building fell down.
At the same time, officials from the US, Ukraine and Europe met in Miami to discuss a plan to end the war.
US envoy Steve Witkoff called the talks constructive, and they covered energy, grain exports and security guarantees.
why: It was the third attack this week in which many civilians died, and the war is now in its fifth year.

stories.title: The US lets Russia sell diesel again to bring down high fuel prices
summary: US President Donald Trump has agreed a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow Russian diesel onto world markets.
Russia will first supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, then 500,000 tonnes in November and more later.
The US Treasury said it would give a temporary licence so that the fuel can be sold despite sanctions.
US diesel reached a record average price of $6.52 a gallon in September, as the war with Iran has largely closed the Strait of Hormuz.
why: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it a weak decision, and the EU said it was not the time to ease pressure on Russia.
Some experts say the amounts are small, because the US alone uses about 3.7 million barrels of diesel a day.

stories.title: Indian police detain more than 1,000 people to stop a protest in New Delhi
summary: Police in New Delhi detained more than 1,000 people on Saturday to stop a large protest against India's chief election official, Gyanesh Kumar.
The protest was called by youth groups, including the Cockroach Janta Party, whose founder Abhijeet Dipke was taken off a plane in Delhi.
Trains to the city were cancelled, mobile internet was switched off, and the main protest site was closed.
A spokesman for the governing BJP said the protest had failed and the country was calm.
why: The protesters say a review of voter lists removed many voters and helped the BJP win some state elections.
Amnesty International called for everyone detained for peaceful protest to be released.

stories.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea blame each other for starting a war
summary: Ethiopia has told the UN Security Council that Eritrea has carried out an all-out invasion of its northern Tigray region.
Ethiopia's foreign minister said Eritrean troops had moved up to 60 kilometres inside the country, and he asked for them to leave.
Eritrea rejected the claim and said Ethiopia had been fighting an unprovoked war against it for more than three years.
Eritrea also accused Ethiopia of wanting to take Assab, an Eritrean port on the Red Sea.
why: Ethiopia lost its coast when Eritrea became independent in 1993, and it has often said it needs access to the sea.
The two neighbours fought a border war from 1998, and they cut diplomatic ties in late September.

stories.title: Taiwan's president says more defence spending is meant to deter war
summary: Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te said in his National Day speech on Saturday that the island wants peace but will not give up its freedom.
He said higher defence spending is meant to deter a war, not to provoke one.
His government has planned a record 1.1 trillion Taiwan dollars, or about US$34.5 billion, for defence in 2027.
China's Taiwan Affairs Office criticised the speech and repeated that Taiwan is part of China.
why: China claims Taiwan, an island of 23 million people, and has not ruled out using force to take control of it.
The holiday marks 115 years since the 1911 uprising that ended China's last imperial dynasty.

stories.title: Report asks why Solomon Islands MPs get medical care overseas while patients wait
summary: An ABC investigation suggests some MPs in Solomon Islands received publicly funded medical treatment abroad when cheaper care was available at home.
In 2025 the prime minister's office spent about $1.5 million on overseas health care for MPs, while about $1.2 million was set aside for ordinary citizens.
Some doctors say they felt pressure from politicians to approve the trips, but the attorney-general said the system is legal.
Prime Minister Matthew Wale said that from next year all such funding will go through a commission with stricter rules.
why: Many citizens must wait or raise money themselves for surgery overseas, such as a young mother with heart disease who needs nearly $35,000.

stories.title: Billionaires and big countries race to the Moon, but who owns it?
summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos's Blue Origin both have plans to build settlements on the Moon.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty says no country can claim the Moon, and it must be used only for peaceful purposes.
However, the treaty says nothing about mining, and a 2015 US law lets American companies own and sell resources they take from space.
So far 76 countries have signed the Artemis Accords, which are led by NASA, but Russia and China have rejected them.
why: Experts say a new, more detailed agreement may be needed, as the UN expects the space industry could be worth a trillion dollars by 2030.

stories.title: High silver prices hurt the makers of traditional wedding shoes in India
summary: In Lucknow, in northern India, craftsmen have made silver wedding shoes called nagras by hand for about 400 years.
The price of silver in India is now about 250,000 rupees per kilogram, more than three times the level of a few years ago.
One shopkeeper said a pair that once cost about $125 now costs over $600, and he has sold nothing for three months.
Many craftsmen have left the trade, and some families now plan to pass old pairs down to new brides.
why: Silver prices rose sharply during the war with Iran, and India also raised its import taxes on silver in May.

stories.title: South African judge Navi Pillay wins the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
summary: The Norwegian Nobel Committee has given the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old judge from South Africa.
Pillay is a former UN human rights chief, and she has worked as a judge at the International Criminal Court and at a UN court for crimes in Rwanda.
The committee said her work had greatly widened the reach of international law.
It chose her from 287 nominations, and it had not yet spoken to her when it announced the prize in Oslo.
why: The committee said that ending conflicts without violence depends on countries following international law.

stories.title: The US puts sanctions on the International Criminal Court
summary: The United States has placed sanctions on the International Criminal Court as a whole, only hours after a former judge of the court won the Nobel Peace Prize.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US would not allow the court to prosecute Americans.
Washington objects to the court's arrest warrants for Israeli leaders, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The measures start in six months, and they could stop banks and other companies from working with the court.
why: The court has 125 member countries, and European Union leaders said they would act to keep it working.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres criticised the decision, while Netanyahu welcomed it.

stories.title: A strong earthquake shakes Panama and causes tsunami warnings
summary: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck near the southern coast of Panama on Friday morning, local time, according to the US Geological Survey.
Warnings of dangerous tsunami waves were issued for several countries on the Pacific coast, and people in Panama City ran out of buildings into the streets.
Damage was reported in central provinces, where a church fell down, but there were no early reports of deaths.
why: President José Raúl Mulino asked people to stay calm.
Several strong aftershocks followed the main earthquake.

stories.title: Houthi missile attack hits the main airport in Saudi Arabia's capital
summary: Yemen's Houthi group says it fired a ballistic missile at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia.
The national airline Saudia said one of its pilots was killed and one of its planes was damaged.
Saudi officials say attacks on the country's airports this week have killed three civilians and injured 36 people.
The airport reopened on Friday, and officials said flights were back to normal.
why: The Houthis, who are backed by Iran, have told airlines to avoid Saudi airspace.
The war in Yemen had been mostly frozen for years, but fighting grew again after the US war on Iran began.

stories.title: AI company Firmus cancels Australia's biggest share sale in decades
summary: Firmus Technologies, a Sydney company that builds data centres for artificial intelligence, has cancelled its plan to list on the Australian stock exchange.
It wanted to raise about $7 billion at a value of $43.7 billion, which would have made it the biggest float since Telstra in 1997.
Some investors said the price was too high, while the company blamed unstable markets.
Chipmaker Nvidia owns 7.2 per cent of Firmus, which now plans to look for private funding and try to list on the Nasdaq next year.
why: The failed sale comes amid fears of an AI bubble, where company values rise much faster than their earnings.

stories.title: Police find two Renoir paintings stolen from a French museum
summary: Two paintings by the French artist Renoir have been found, and six people have been arrested, officials in southern France said on Friday.
The paintings, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Young Woman at the Well, were taken from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer last month.
The thieves cut through a fence and climbed in through a window, and the robbery lasted less than three minutes.
They took four paintings but left two of them behind as they escaped.
why: The town's mayor, Bryan Masson, said the paintings are part of the town's heritage.
The theft has led to new calls for better security at museums in France, a year after jewels were stolen from the Louvre in Paris.

stories.title: Birds return to an Australian reef island once destroyed by mining
summary: Lady Elliot Island, a small coral island at the southern end of the Great Barrier Reef, was stripped bare by guano mining more than 150 years ago.
Miners removed about 20,000 tonnes of guano, which is seabird droppings used as fertiliser, and the island stayed almost empty of plants for more than 100 years.
Families who ran tourism on the island have planted more than 20,000 trees, and the work is now about 70 per cent complete.
About 100,000 black noddies, a type of seabird, now nest there each year, up from only a few thousand about 60 years ago.
why: A researcher called it an extraordinary recovery, and it shows that damaged nature can come back with long-term care.

stories.title: A Russian strike on a bus stop in eastern Ukraine kills at least 33 people
summary: A Russian glide bomb hit two city buses at a bus stop in Kramatorsk, a city near the front line in eastern Ukraine, killing at least 33 people and wounding 18, according to Ukrainian officials.
City officials said there were no military targets nearby, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack would not go unanswered.
It came a day after a missile hit an apartment block in the northern town of Pryluky and killed 22 people.
why: Peace talks have stalled because Russia wants Ukraine to give up the rest of the Donetsk region, which Kyiv refuses to do.
The United Nations has confirmed more than 17,000 civilian deaths since 2022 and says the real number is much higher.

stories.title: Oil climbs above $100 as attacks on tankers revive fears for Gulf supplies
summary: Brent crude oil rose to about US$101 a barrel in early trading on Thursday after a rise in attacks on ships in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
On Wall Street, shares slipped from record highs, and US government bond yields climbed to their highest level in 24 years.
Investors worry that expensive oil will push up inflation and keep interest rates high.
why: A large share of the world's oil travels through the Strait of Hormuz, so even small disruptions can raise fuel prices everywhere.
Last week the G7 and the International Energy Agency agreed to release 100 million barrels of crude oil and diesel from reserves to calm the market.

stories.title: WHO presses Russia for answers after a fatal plague case in Siberia
summary: A 28-year-old woman who worked at a plague research institute in Irkutsk, Siberia, has died of what doctors suspect was pneumonic plague, the most dangerous form of the disease.
Russian media then reported a second worker with an unexplained pneumonia, but the Kremlin called most of the reports false and health officials said no staff were infected.
The World Health Organization has asked Russia for a formal response and says it still does not know the source of the infection.
why: Under international health rules, countries are expected to report quickly any outbreak that could spread to other countries.
Plague can be treated with antibiotics if it is found early.

stories.title: Canadian poet Anne Carson wins the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
summary: Anne Carson, a 76-year-old poet and essayist from Toronto, has won this year's Nobel Prize in Literature.
The Swedish Academy praised her bold and inventive work, which plays with ancient Greek and Roman literature and mixes poetry, essay and fiction in new forms.
Her best-known books include Autobiography of Red, a novel written in verse, and the prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or about US$1.7 million.
why: Carson was in Iceland when the news came and was very surprised, according to the Academy.
She is also known for her translations of ancient Greek poetry, including the work of Sappho.

stories.title: Japan's competition watchdog raids the country's four biggest beer makers
summary: Japan's Fair Trade Commission has raided Asahi, Kirin, Sapporo and Suntory, which together sell about 90 per cent of the beer in Japan.
The watchdog is investigating whether the companies acted as a cartel by raising prices at the same time over several years, blaming costs such as raw materials.
All four brewers said they would cooperate, and shares in three of them fell nearly 4 per cent after the raids were reported.
why: Competition laws ban rival companies from agreeing on prices, because that can make customers pay more.
If the commission finds the law was broken, it can file a criminal complaint.

stories.title: Indonesians take their government to court over months of wildfire smoke
summary: Community groups in West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, have sued Indonesia's president, ministers and local leaders, saying the government failed to deal with peatland fires and the haze they create.
The fires began in July, and the Health Ministry has recorded at least 175,000 cases of respiratory infections linked to the smoke since August.
The groups want the fires declared a national emergency, free health care for vulnerable people, and those responsible to be prosecuted.
why: Smoke from Indonesian fires often drifts to Singapore and Malaysia, and burning peatland releases large amounts of carbon.
Police say they have named 196 suspects and are investigating 96 companies, but the rainy season is not expected in most areas until November.

stories.title: China gives AI 'digital humans' their own ID cards
summary: Beijing is testing a programme that gives identity cards to AI digital humans, the computer-made characters that appear in ads, videos and livestreams.
The first card went to a virtual pop idol called Yuri, and it records a name, birthday, address and facial features.
Supporters say registration will protect intellectual property and fight online scams, while critics warn it could expand state surveillance.
why: At least 1.3 million Chinese companies are linked to the digital human industry, which was worth about 48 billion yuan, or US$10 billion, in 2025.

stories.title: Taiwan moves toward restarting nuclear power as AI drives up electricity demand
summary: Taiwan's Nuclear Safety Commission has finished reviewing plans to restart the Maanshan nuclear power plant, which was shut down in May 2025.
If safety checks go well, the plant could produce power again as early as 2028, helping to meet rising demand from chip factories, data centres and artificial intelligence.
Taiwan imports about 96 per cent of its energy, and last year gas and coal produced more than 80 per cent of its electricity.
why: Taiwan turned away from nuclear power after Japan's Fukushima disaster in 2011, so a restart would be a major change in policy.
Critics say the plant is too small to make a big difference and that the problem of radioactive waste is still unsolved.
